Totally — I think independent commissions are the most leverage-y reform. They stop the distortion at the source and make every other fix (voter access, campaign finance, etc.) more likely to translate into real representation.

A couple thoughts on what makes a commission effective:
- genuinely independent appointment process (mix of branches/actors, limits on partisan insiders)
- clear, enforceable criteria (compactness, respect for communities of interest, preserving cores of existing districts) and bans on using partisan data or incumbent addresses
- transparency: public hearings, published mapping data, open-source tools
- judicial review/backstops so courts can step in if lines are abusive
- ongoing audits and opportunities for public input so maps aren’t cooked behind closed doors

Politically, ballot initiatives can work where legislatures are blocked, but that takes well-run grassroots campaigns and clear messaging about how reform benefits voters. Where legislatures are amenable, pushing through statutory or constitutional changes is faster but harder politically.

I’d pair redistricting reform with campaigns to expand voter access and public financing — those complement each other. As a researcher I’m also drawn to using rigorous, easy-to-understand metrics and demos to show voters the before/after effects of gerrymandering.
